Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent? The current Russian military doesn’t just seem incompetent — they are incompetent. And corrupt — from top to bottom. A Russian contract soldier who deserted and escaped to the West told about the disarray and corruption in the Russian army to Verstka Media. Anton (not his real name) decided to sign a contract with the Russian army to pay off the debts. Anton was struggling to repay loans amounting to 1 million ruble ($10,000). In Russia, most people don’t earn such money in a year. It were the bailiffs who convinced Anton to sign up for the war in Ukraine. Ads for army contract service are plastered all over Russia. (Stock photos are used throughout this post.) The conditions they offered sounded great: a contract with the civil organization JSC Investinform (it gets paid for recruiting soldiers for the war with Ukraine), plus the regional payout on sign up, plus payments from the Ministry of Defense. In total, Anton was supposed to be earning about 350,000 rub. per month ($3,500). In August 2023, Anton arrived in Moscow, signed a 1-year contract with the Ministry of Defense and an employment contract with JSC Investinform. The second contract allowed him to get top-up payments in addition to the standard 215,000 rub. ($2,150) MOD wage to Russian soldiers in Ukraine. That’s how Moscow officials meet the allocated quotas of soldiers per region: on paper, these recruits are Muscovites, but in reality, it’s deprived residents of small Russian towns living in poverty that are sent to the war. Muscovites have no desire to die for Putin; they live quite well. Think ‘Hunger Games’ districts and the Capitol: that’s Russia and Moscow. On sign up, Anton was immediately paid 400,000 rub. ($4,000). All debt collection proceedings against him had been suspended — that’s another “perk” offered to desperate Russians in need, to convince them to sign up for the war. However, he couldn’t use the money to repay the debts. Instead, he was forced to spend the money he got upfront to buy a proper uniform and personal protective equipment — bulletproof helmet, vest, etc. When new recruits arrived to the army training grounds, they were given some ancient uniforms and combat boots — all of them were 4–6 sizes too large. The helmet was from the times of WWII, a piece of shrapnel would pierce it like paper. But as soon as they arrived to barracks, helpful “intermediates” arrived, eager to sell to the fresh recruits all they needed. Nothing in the Russian army was for free. If you came to “earn big money”, you first needed to buy your own gear. The newbies had to pay the full retail price for their clothing and equipment. On top of that, they had to pay for parts for the machinery they would be using in the future. Some lame excuse was offered to make them pay for parts. Basically, commanders know how much cash you have been just paid, and extract it all before you have a chance to spend it. $4,000 went quick. The workers of the military warehouse where they were supposed to get equipment and uniforms were all drunk. Half of the officers were drunk as well. Quickly the recruits learned that they had to buy not only their own military gear but also food: within 2 weeks, all soldiers got food poisoning from eating the meals in the military canteen. So, they had to buy food in the local kiosk, where a liter of milk cost $8. The shop assistant was driving a luxury Mercedes, Anton says. Corruption in the Russian army is all-permeating. Because of Anton’s vocal complaints about the equipment, he was sent to a “Storm-Z” unit after the training course. Storm-Z is the “penal brigades”, where murderers and robbers recruited from prisons and deserters who were caught are shipped. Out of 600 recruits delivered to the front with him, only 40 survived after 2 months of assaults near Kupyansk. “It was just some kind of extermination. From one company, 5–6 people would return alive. The tanks and armored carriers were also smashed. In the end, we were mixed with prisoners and were simply pushed, pushed, pushed ahead.” How did he survive? “How I survived is a good question. I was a grenade launcher, not a stormtrooper, I didn’t go in attacks. We operated from hidden positions. Direct fire in these fields is not an option,” recalls Anton. “In 9 cases out of 10, storm troops are liquidated on approach.” “There are no experienced people in the infantry; people run away. If a person survives, he refuses to go on attacks, he starts having anxiety and hysterics. People rather go to jail than go on attacks.” In the village of Zaytsevo (Luhansk region), there is an unofficial jail where the Russians are holding soldiers who refused to continue to fight. Some of them say it’s “hell”, but it surely beats dying under heavy artillery fire trying to storm fortified Ukrainian positions. “The losses were simply insane, I lost count. For 3 kilometers, which were eventually taken back by the Ukrainians, 5–6 companies were killed,” According to Anton, the commanders are reprimanded for heavy losses, so all of those who haven’t returned from the attack are reported as “missing” (presumed deserters), not killed. Anton was deployed from the beginning of October till the end of November 2023. By that time, only a few people were left in his unit. They were taken in the rear of Russia-occupied Luhansk region, where they had to train the new recruits — prisoners and contractors. Then suddenly they were loaded on trucks and shipped to a camp in the Belgorod region (Russian territory near the border with Kharkiv region of Ukraine). By mid-March 2024, they were sent on the location near the Ukrainian border. Their unit was loaded on trucks (most Russian armed personnel carriers are destroyed by now, the troops are moved around by trucks) and for the whole night and the next day their column was driving on roads. Anton didn’t know that a raid by “Freedom of Russia Legion” was ongoing in the Belgorod region for already 3 days. He says that their commanders also didn’t know what was going on. Their trucks got under artillery fire. One of Anton’s colleagues was killed in a strike. His group hid at a cottage of a 90-year-old granny. No one knew what to do, commanders didn’t give any orders. They were under fire for several hours. Only the next morning the commanders contacted them and told them where to go. By that time, all locals escaped the village, stores and offices didn’t operate. The soldiers were ordered to stay in the local school, which was also closed. The soldiers simply hid there and slept. Communication with the base wasn’t working. They were under artillery fire, drones circling above the place. “We heard the conversations of our comrades, but we could not answer. There was an attack and breakthrough at their positions. Not only Storm-Z units were there but also border guards. In the meantime, it turned out that a whole platoon had been demolished in the woods.” Later the same day Anton went with a group to evacuate the wounded and dead from the battlefield — he had to replace the deceased colleague, although he hadn’t done evacuations before. During the evacuation, the group had to shed their weapons and armor, which weighed up to 50 kg, and walked 5 km back to the school. (The wounded guy that Anton evacuated died in the hospital.) In the basement, where the school canteen was, they took some sleep. As they woke up, they had to go back to get their weapons. Anton marked the location where he hid his grenade launcher on the map with an asterisk. “If I lost the grenade launcher, I would be transferred to the infantry, and infantry means certain death. Machine guns and rifles are dime a dozen, but it’s nearly impossible to procure something mightier.” Anton says that once his commander opened up and blurted: “I don’t give a f**k about you contractors, they’ll send me as many of you as I need — but for the lost equipment I would be hauled over the coals, it’s a lot of paperwork.” In storm troops, losses reach up to 90%, says Anton. He believes that if it weren’t for aerial bombing by the Russian Air Forces, the units of Russians that are fighting for Ukraine (“Freedom of Russia” Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, who were responsible for the raid on the Russian territory) would have easily captured the border areas of the Belgorod region with the help of FPV drones and artillery. Ukraine is superior to Russia by half a century in technical terms, their artillery is more accurate, and drones constantly conduct reconnaissance, Anton says. After the raid, the commander of Anton’s unit went on a drinking binge — along with his entire headquarters. The commander blamed the signalman for the failure in communications and began beating him up — after a few days of the torture, the signalman deserted. Meanwhile, Anton himself was thinking about doing the same thing. At the end of March 2024, he was watching a video of Russian oppositional channel ‘TV Dozhd’ (they were banned in Russia in 2022 and now broadcast from Europe), which mentioned the organization that helped Russian soldiers to escape the army and desert from the front (‘Idite Lesom’). At first he was skeptical, but when rumors about an upcoming offensive in the Kharkiv region spread, decided to give it a go. Anton says he realized that it’s impossible to survive in the Russian storm troops. Before agreeing to sign the contract, he had completely different ideas what it would be like. He asked the commanders to take 3 days off, but they refused. He couldn’t get a leave either — he says that even mobilized soldiers who serve since September 2022 can’t get a vacation. But he managed to get commanders’ permission to leave the unit for 1 night — until the morning. “Almost everyone who has been behind the front line thinks about escaping,” says Anton. 1.5 months after his escape, he cannot adapt to the peaceful life in a safe European country. Sometimes he has panic attacks and adrenaline rushes, but he tries to suppress them. His attitude towards the war in Ukraine has changed greatly. “There is guilt on me,” admits Anton. ”Once, our detachment commander broke down, drunk: “Yes, we are f***ing orcs!” “It’s disillusionment. The commanders don’t show it, and such coming outs happen mainly because they are drunk. During my time there, my entire outlook on life changed. I no longer feel anything positive about the Russian state. This is not a war, but some kind of agony. The only parallels that emerge are with the World War 1. We are simply being sent to slaughter,” concludes Anton. He plans to stay in Europe and apply for political asylum. He believes that he has the right to claim it as “a person who refused to participate in war crimes.” He never fully repaid the loans — and has no plans to do it.

Even defiant actions like attending the funeral of the leader of opposition Alexei Navalny, killed by Putin’s regime in February 2024 (attending a funeral is technically not against the law) can still create substantial consequences for the participants. 16 thousand people came to the funeral of Alexei Navalny in Moscow on March 1, 2024. Thousands more came to lay flowers in the following days. The FSB films such events and identifies the attendees, and then begins “working” on them. There are hundreds of thousands — possibly, millions — of people in Russia who who support Ukraine and are against Putin's actions in Eastern Europe. They are just saying nothing. But even those who show support for the war — as required by the state — aren’t going to be upset if the war ends tomorrow, and they don’t care about “Russia’s victory” — as the Soviet people didn’t care about “the USSR victory” when a withdrawal of the Soviet troops from Afghanistan was announced in 1989, after a 10-year “international duty mission”. 1989: Withdrawal of the Soviet troops from Afghanistan. Literally, if Putin died today and his successor announced that Russia is withdrawing troops from Ukraine, the vast majority of Russians would breathe a huge sigh of relief. Everyone in Russia is tired of this war. Even the guy who started it all.

What do Russians think about Putin's wartime policies? Dmitry Grinchiy was born in the infamous year 1937 — the year of Stalin’s ‘Great Purge’. Just a few months after little Dmitry was born, his father Pavel Grinchiy was arrested by the NKVD. In 1938, Pavel Grinchiy was shot as ‘the enemy of the people.’ Just like a million of other Soviet citizens were shot. At the time, the Soviet people zealously supported the fight against "enemies of the people." Stalin’s propagandists repeated every day that “enemies and spies are everywhere”, and that “we must remain vigilant.” And the Soviet people were vigilant. They wrote millions of reports to the NKVD, pointing out potential “enemies of the people”. In all probabilities, Pavel Grinchiy was shot because someone he knew reported on him. 87 years have passed. Dmitry Grinchiy (who never even got to know his own father, killed on Stalin’s orders), lived his life in the USSR — through the collapse of the USSR, through “terrible 1990s” and the 25 years of Putin’s regime, from its inception to the fated launch of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In 2024, he found himself in a country where the regime every day tells the citizens that “enemies and spies are everywhere” and that “we must be vigilant”. And the Russian people are vigilant. Yesterday, 2 such vigilant Russian citizens attacked Dmitry Grinchiy on a bus in Moscow, they beat him up and dragged him to a police station. (Video in the comments below.) The 2 vigilantes decided that Grinchiy was “an enemy of the people” simply because (in their view) Grinchy said something “disrespectful” about the monument to “Wagner” — the chief of which, Yevgeny Prigozhin, was, by the way, killed on Putin’s orders after an attempt of armed rebellion. Some say that the recent incursion by the Ukrainian forces may lead to another “Justice March” towards Moscow. Fortunately for Grinchiy, the police decided to release him. Maybe because they didn’t want to lock up the old man immediately — the Russian prosecution machine has a habit of charging and locking up people after some time, even though initially the accused have been released after being detained and questioned. It’s unlikely the vigilantes will get as much as a slap in the wrist, after beating the old man. I’m shocked how quickly — in front of my eyes — Russia turned from a country pretending to be a semi-liberal democracy into a full-blown militaristic dictatorship, where people write reports on friends and family for “saying wrong things”, where books are being burned, with non-stop hateful propaganda from every screen. I’m shocked — but the majority of Russians are earnestly embracing “the new realities” with vigor and dedication not seen since 1937.

What does Putin's reaction (or lack thereof) to the events in the Kursk region reveal about his hold on power in Russia? Putin even kissed the Quran, to secure Kadyrov’s support. (Video in the comments below.) Which is really weird, because Putin claims to be an Orthodox Christian. If he is a Christian, then kissing Quran is a double sacrilege — both for Christians and for Muslims. And if Putin has secretly taken Islam (his secret de-facto wife Alina Kabaeva is Tatar, and most Tatars are Muslims), then why does Putin still go to Christian churches and crosses himself? Also Putin a day ago, vigorously crossing himself. By all signs, Putin is getting ready for some major internal happening. Kadyrov’s units are part of Russia’s “National Guard” ‘Rosgvardia’, which is the internal army exclusively managed by the president, but even within that department Kadyrovets have a special privileged status. And Putin is unsure that his “stormtrooper” is still fully behind him. Follow me for more updates!

Will the USA continue to support Ukraine after Trump takes office? No one knows for sure, but Ukrainians don’t seem to believe in Trump’s best intentions about “ending the war in Ukraine in 24 hours.” “Trump is Putin’s asset,” is a belief shared by a large part of Ukrainians and the Russian opposition in exile. Not many hold a hope that Ukraine’s sovereignty will be strongly protected by the Trump administration. In a poll by Kyiv-based blogger Michael Sheitelman, 73% of the respondents said that they believe that Kamala Harris will be the next president of the United States. Nearly 20,000 respondents took part in the online poll. Donald Trump is known for his unpredictability, but from what he previously said, it doesn’t appear for Ukrainians that their country would be better off with Donald Trump at the Oval Office. Vice versus, most Ukrainians fear that Trump will simply cut the American financial and military support to Ukraine, and force Ukrainians to surrender 4 seashore regions and the occupied Crimea to Russia. Ukraine’s president Zelensky spoke to Donald Trump, following his nomination as the Republican candidate in the aftermath of the assassination attempt. Former British prime-minister Boris Johnson also spoke to Trump about the importance of Ukraine for the global security. "Whatever some other Republicans may have said about Ukraine in the past, I believe that Trump understands the reality: that a defeat for Ukraine would be a massive defeat for America,” stated Johnson after the conversation. ”I believe that Trump can end it — on the right terms for Ukraine and the West,” concludes Johnson. And how would he do it? ”There is only one way to achieve this outcome — through strength. Washington under Trump will have to show that international borders must be respected, and that the Soviet empire cannot be rebuilt by force,” asserts Johnson. ”A win for Ukraine — properly handled — could pave the way, paradoxically, for a new and far better relationship with Russia. That would be a big win, for America and for the whole world.” As I said, no one knows for sure, whether the USA will continue to support Ukraine after Trump takes office and what he would actually do — and that’s one thing that is probably making Vladimir Putin and his gang very nervous. Follow me for more updates!

How likely is it that Evan Gershkovich will be released from prison in Russia soon? Evan Gershkovich may be able to return home soon, with some promising movements in Russia — in the past couple of weeks, several high-profile political prisoners disappeared from Russian jails. This sparked rumors about a potential prisoner exchange — prisoners “disappear” when they are moved from their prisons. Unannounced prisoner exchanges happen often. Especially if there are multiple prisoners swapped, both sides usually prefer to keep it secret until the exchange actually occurs. Political prisoners who disappeared from their prisons: On July 19, after American journalist Evan Gershkovich was sentenced to 16 years for simply doing his job (Russia accused him of “spying”), President Biden stated: ”Evan has endured his ordeal with remarkable strength. We will not cease in our efforts to bring him home.” It’s possible that these efforts produced results, and there is indeed a prisoner swap happening soon.

Why did Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visit Ukraine? India’s prime minister Narendra Modi brought a mobile hospital for Ukrainians, who are fighting off the Russian invasion for 2.5 years. In the book of honored guests at Kyiv’s Mariinsky Palace, Modi wrote, “On behalf of the people of India, whose population is 1.4 billion people, I pray for peace, progress and prosperity for the friendly people of Ukraine." It was the first ever visit of the head of the Indian government to Ukraine, since it gained independence in 1991. Ukraine president Zelenskyy and prime minister Modi visited the National Museum of History of Ukraine, showing the story of the Russian invasion since February 2022 and how it affected Ukrainians, particularly kids. Modi was visibly moved. Modi told Zelensky that he personally is ready to assist to achieve peace in Ukraine. India immediately "stood on the side of peace," said Modi to Zelenskyy. In a peaceful settlement, respect for sovereignty and integrity are priorities, he added. There were 4 agreements signed between India and Ukraine, covering medical field, agricultural cooperation, humanitarian relations, and culture. “Following the visit, we also agreed on a joint statement focusing on the development of a strategic partnership, bilateral trade, and continued military-technical cooperation,” posted president Zelenskyy. “India supports Ukraine's national sovereignty and territorial integrity. And this is critical because everyone in the world must equally respect the UN Charter,” Zelenskyy emphasized. Modi and Zelenskyy met previously in June in Italy during G7 summit. Following that meeting, Modi visited Putin in Russia, but cut his visit short and left one day earlier than he planned. (During Modi’s visit to Moscow, Russia hit children’s hospital in Kyiv.) Modi also met with members of the Indian community in Ukraine, who live and work there. Many Indians were going to Ukraine to study, particularly medicine and engineering. After completing their studies, some of them stayed in the country, started businesses there. At the start of the war in February 2022, 18,000 Indian students studied in Ukraine and were evacuated. Many of them since returned and now continue their studies, others are waiting until the war ends. To get a degree in Ukraine is more than twice cheaper, that’s why so many foreign students (not only from India but from many other countries) used to choose to study there. India benefited greatly from Russia’s isolated status due to western sanctions, allowing India to purchase oil from Russia at heavy discount. At the same time, India sharply decreased its purchases of Russia’s weapons and equipment, and began buying more weapons from the West. For India, western support is important, as China is striving for more influence in the region, simultaneously supplying weapons to India’s enemy Pakistan. For Ukraine, India’s support as a nation of 1.4 billion people is substantial. India has yet joined the June 2024 Swiss Peace Summit resolution, which outlined the framework of just peace for Ukraine.

Has Omsk oil refinery, Russia's largest oil refinery just caught fire and has blown up? Gazprom, local news. How much will this affect Russia's diesel, petrol, aviation and hydrofuels? How far is Umsk from Kiev? Is Palianytsia suspected? The explosion at the Omsk oil refinery yesterday was powerful — windows were blown out in nearby houses. According to Reuters, as a result of the explosion and subsequent fire at the Omsk oil refinery, the AVT-11 primary oil refining unit — most productive at the plant — was damaged and had to be shot down. That’s half of the plant's capacity. The fire area affected over 1,000 square meters. Omsk is about 3,000 km away from Ukraine and it’s unlikely the explosion was the result of a drone attack — although the new Ukrainian jet drone ‘Palianytsia’ can potentially fly that far, some experts believe. If Ukraine were able to hit this far (with a jet drone or another weapon), it would be a completely different reality that Russians would have to exist in.

What if the Kursk disaster in 2000 had prevented Putin from getting to power? How would Russia have looked today? Vladimir Putin’s presidential term started with Kursk nuclear submarine disaster on 12 August 2000. The submarine sank in the Barents Sea and all 118 personnel on board perished. The crews of nearby ships, which all were taking part in a large-scale naval exercise, felt two explosions, but the generals did not start any search for the vessel for 6 hours. The explosion was so powerful, it was recorded by seismologists in Alaska. It took over 16 hours to locate the submarine (the emergency rescue buoy had been switched off). It was finally located on the ocean floor at a depth of 108 metres (354 ft). Newly inaugurated Putin was on holiday and refused to cut his vacation short, to deal with the crisis. After the explosions, 23 sailors remained alive on the submarine — they died waiting to be rescued. Putin was refusing to allow foreigners to be part of the rescue mission, and Russians were unable to do what was needed to be done. Desperate relatives were waiting for news about their men at the quayside, growing more and more despondent because of the inaction by the state officials and the Navy. All this time Russian officials lied about what was happening. “The communication with the crew has been established, they are getting hot food!” was telling the Navy spokesman. Blatant lies. Only on August 20 — 8 days after the catastrophe — the Norwegian vessel ‘Seaway Eagle’ was allowed to begin working on the recovery mission. Norwegian divers did in 24 hours what the Russians could not do in a week — they managed to open the submarine's emergency escape hatch. But it was too late. All survivors of the accident were already dead. When the Russian TV — which was still reporting freely at the time — done an investigative piece on the tragedy and showed the widows of the marines, Putin accused the program in ”hiring whores for $10” to discredit him: “You hire whores on purpose. You gave them 10 dollars each, specifically to discredit me,” Putin claimed. It was after the Kursk disaster that Putin began raider seizures of the independent media. This was 24 years ago. Today, the words “Kursk” and “Putin” are again in the news, but this time it’s the Kursk region of Russia — and the Ukrainian troops’ incursion into Russia. And once again, Putin is lying about it. But this no longer surprises anyone. ”Kursk” disaster didn’t cripple Putin’s grasp on power — but maybe, Kursk will?

How likely is it that Ukraine has secretly prepared dirty bombs with nuclear material as a last line of defence against the Russian nuclear attack? Every time the questions about “dirty bombs” pop up on Quora, it coincides with the intel on Russia’s discussing the covert use of tactical nukes in their fight against Ukraine. The Russian propagandists openly talked about nuking Ukrainian troops on the territory of Russia, following the Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region. What is happening in Kursk is so embarrassing that Russian propagandists couldn’t help bragging about Russia’s nuclear prowess. And the idea of Russia’s nuking its own territory isn’t new either — Margarita Simonyan, the chief editor of ‘Russia Today’ propaganda center, talked about it already in October 2023, explaining that Russia has full right to blow a nuke in the air over the Russian territory. Meanwhile, this is reportedly a warehouse of Russian nuclear warheads. This rotten garbage is more likely to explode at the first touch than to fly anywhere. That’s more likely to act as a “dirty bomb.” And apparently, Russia is full of such warehouses — especially the European regions near the border. This is what everyone — especially Russians — should be worried about, and not some mythical “dirty bomb” made by Ukrainians.

Is the West now negotiating with Putin or is it too vain? Putin is seeking peace and has made an offer to negotiate on the basis of the current situation on the battlefield. So the ball is in Ukraine's court. Except for Kremlin bots, no one pays much attention to Putin’s blabbing anymore. At some stage, you no longer find it ridiculous or absurd, but can’t help feeling that you see a seriously mentally disturbed individual who needs professional help. Putin keeps saying the same things in his speeches most of the time, and the only reason people took notice of his yesterday’s “peace proposal” to Ukraine was because Putin demanded that Ukraine withdrew from the territories it controls — and just gave them to Russia. In fact, Putin’s demand to give him the city of Kherson is probably the first case in the history of mankind when an invader demands to give him the territory from which his own army fled in disgrace. Just imagine. 1943. Germany is stuck on the eastern front in Ukraine. And here the Fuhrer proposes: alright, we are ready to negotiate, but only if the Red Army first withdraws beyond the Urals — and right up to the Urals there will be Nazi Reich. That’s the value of Putin’s “peace proposal”, in a nutshell. In fact, anyone calling Putin’s ultimatum “a peace plan” is either on Kremlin’s payout or have their own agenda: invading someone’s country and then demanding to keep their land is a “peace plan” to the same degree as mugging someone at gunpoint is a “business plan.” Putin's requests about Ukraine’s surrender haven’t been discussed at the G7 summit and were not taken seriously, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz said in an interview with ZDF. Not sure how soon the exhausted mind of Vladimir Putin will have a chance to get the professional help it needs, but Putin’s loss of touch with reality hasn’t affected these around him to the same extent. In the occupied Crimea, Russians are getting ready to do a runner: the heads of Crimean museums received letters from the Ministry of Culture, ordering them to prepare museum valuables for “evacuation.” Putin may be putting up a brave front, but his officials are busy looting and stealing what they can, before they are kicked out of Crimea. Except for Putin, everyone understands what is going to happen next.

How could Ukraine invading the Kursk region in Russia be an embarrassment to President Vladimir Putin? Vladimir Putin’s plane landing in Kursk, to support the region in fighting off Ukraine’s invasion. JUST KIDDING!! Putin flew to Baku, Azerbaijan, while 18–19-year-old Russian conscripts are flown by military planes to the Kursk region from all over Russia. Putin never goes to where problems in Russia happen — be it a major flood or an invasion by a foreign power. Putin doesn’t want to associate himself with disasters. He only wants to associate himself with victories. Putin needs to redirect attention from the invasion of Kursk and Belgorod, and the meager response provided by the Russian military. For 2 weeks, Russia — a nuclear power — cannot repel foreign troops that invaded its territory. Moreover, that’s another “red line” crossed — and nothing is happening! The world realized that there are no “red lines”. The king is naked. And this is obvious not only to westerners but also to Russian citizens who previously believed the TV, promoting Russia’s “greatness”. Moreover, Kursk locals who didn’t evacuate, got to see Ukrainians, fighting against the Russian army. They saw that they are not “Nazis”, but normal guys, who are also handing out humanitarian aid — food, water. They also saw that the local administration and police were the first to run away, leaving them alone with the "enemy". That there was no evacuation. They also saw how the Russian TV was showing completely different scenes. People saw that they are being lied to. Mothers of Russian conscripts who are serving the compulsory 1-year-term of military service got a shock of their lives that their sons can be placed in mortal danger, despite many promises made by Vladimir Putin that conscripts won’t be involved in combat. There are about 350,000 conscripts in the Russian army and they all have mothers, fathers, siblings, grandparents. All these families are now terrified that their teens who were promised that they wouldn’t be fighting the Ukrainians, could be fed into the meat grinder of the war. Despite Putin’s hopes and requests of Duma members, there are no queues to army recruitment centers to “defend the Russian land from invaders”. And this must be the most embarrassing thing for Putin.

What do you think will happen as fighting rages on in Russia's Kursk region? A Russian soldier’s chevron proclaims, “Like it or not, but Russia is expanding,” echoing a popular folk adage. Ironically, the soldier was captured by the Ukrainian troops, expanding the zone of Ukraine’s occupation in Russia. (Video in the comments below.) In 18 days, Ukraine managed to capture around 1,300 square km in the heavily-populated region of Kursk in Central Russia. Ukraine invaded Russia on August 6, 2024, and for over 2 weeks, there is nothing that the Russian army can do to repel the surprise invasion of the “sacred Russian land.” Vice versus, the Ukrainian army keeps capturing 1–3 villages daily, and there are already 94 settlements under their control. The Ukrainian army established military administration on the occupied territories, to ensure order and manage humanitarian assistance to remaining residents: as many as 130,000 residents evacuated from the occupied towns to Russia (as reported by the Russian side), with around 20,000 Kursk region residents remaining on the Ukraine-controlled territory. There is also a curfew from 5 pm to 10 am, introduced by the Ukrainian military administration, giving residents only 7 hours during which they can get out of their homes. Initially, Russian leaders didn’t treat Ukraine’s incursion into the Kursk region seriously and ordered to use compulsory draftees aged 18–19 to plug the holes, instead of moving experienced units of contract soldiers from the territory of Ukraine. Now, reports are surfacing that units of the Russian army are starting to be moved, to be used on the territory of the Kursk Oblast, tasked with the goal of squeezing out the Ukrainian forces. This is opening the opportunity for the Ukrainian units standing against Russians in Ukraine to increase counterattacks on the territory of partially occupied Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk regions — and apparently, the Ukrainian forces are already using these gaps. We’ll hear more in the coming days. So, the Kursk operation is only a part of a bigger plan by the Ukrainian commander-in-chief to seize the initiative. Apparently, Ukrainians used a brand-new weapon to target the Voronezh site — a jet-powered drone ‘Palyanitsia’. Each of these strikes is a stroke of a global plan. We are not seeing isolated, random attempts at attacks. We are witnessing the implementation of carefully orchestrated series of operations within the framework of a single plan. What is the main goal of the plan? To force the Russian troops to leave Ukraine.

What will be the effects of all the purges Putin is doing to the Russian Army? Putin’s purge of the Russian army generals continues: The commander of the 20th Army Sukhrab Akhmedov has been removed from his post. Also yesterday, the head of the Department of Defense Procurement, Vladimir Verteletsky, was arrested and accused of bribery. Verteletsky is accused of taking a bribe “of an especially large scale”: allegedly, he received a car and a house from an entrepreneur working with state defense orders. The house was registered in the name of Verteletsky’s family member. His arrest continues the string of scandalous detainments of top military generals and executives of Russia’s ministry of defence. 4 previously arrested generals and ministry of defence execs: army generals Popov and Shamarin, Shoigu’s deputies Ivanov and Kuznetsov. A source in the Lefortovo prison in Moscow, controlled by the FSB, tipped that a special section was being prepared for impending mass arrests of army generals. The cells are being equipped with high-tech listening devices to pick up even the quietest of whispers. By the looks of it, paranoid Putin is trying to avoid another military coup, similar to the one of Yevgeny Prigozhin’s in June 2023. There is a lot of dissent among the ranks of the military, and at some time or another, probably all generals cursed their superiors and Putin himself. Such criticism of Putin used to be the norm in private conversations between army generals, but that was last year. Now any dissent can land you behind the bars. Seems like Putin is planning something so heinous, he wants to make sure that the chain of command is unbreakable — that no one will say, “No, I’m not doing it.” A lot of army generals are probably now wishing they supported Prigozhin a year ago, and not just stood aside.

Is Hungary refusing to send Ukraine weapons because Putin has Orban in his pocket? Hungarian opposition politician Peter Magyar was the main challenger to Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s party at the last election to the European parliament — and after Russia hit the largest children's hospital in Ukraine, Magyar traveled to Kyiv to deliver humanitarian aid. Magyar's party collected about 15 million forints (USD $41,000) donated by Hungarians and gathered medical supplies for the Kyiv hospital destroyed by the Russian strike — literally at the time when Orban was in China, demanding “peace in Ukraine”, meaning that Ukrainians should stop resisting the Russian invasion and give in to Putin’s demands. Magyar is skeptical about the success of Orban’s “peace mission”: "The prime minister is allowed to travel the world and pretend that he is creating peace [...] but we believe in actions instead of flying around the world 3 times. We are different," Magyar said. Today, Magyar visited a memorial to victims of the Bucha Massacre near Kyiv. However, in the question of supporting military aid for Ukraine, Magyar also states he doesn’t want weapons to be delivered to Ukraine via the Hungarian territory or for Hungary to send any of its own military supplies for the Ukrainian troops. Magyar explains that if Hungary were to support Ukraine militarily, then the areas of Ukraine where people with Hungarian roots live could he hit by the Russian missiles. That’s an interesting statement: sounds like Putin promised to the Hungarian leadership not to strike Ukrainian towns near the Hungarian border if Hungary refrains from supporting Ukraine’s military effort. Ukraine borders 7 countries: Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Moldova, Russia, and Belarus. If what Magyar says is true, other European leaders would have been given the same info. If all these countries had blocked the delivery of weapons to Ukraine, it would be left defenseless. Now, we know that Poland is a fierce supporter of Ukraine, and that explains why Putin is so bitter about Poles. Coming back to Magyar, the difference between him and Orban is that the oppositional politician doesn’t object military aid to Ukraine, provided by other countries. It is the party led by Magyar that was behind the massive anti-Orban, anti-Putin protests in Hungary. Magyar’s party TISZA (Respect and Freedom) is building momentum to win over Orbán in the next national elections, scheduled for 2026.

How much support does Vladimir Putin have for the invasion of Ukraine among his own people? This Russian soldier who lost his limb in Ukraine complains that he didn’t receive the payments of 3 million rub. (USD $30,000) for the heavy injury and 812,000 rub. ($8,120) for disability, which were promised by recruiters. He says that “the other guys” who served with him didn’t get payments either. His last hope to get paid what they were promised was to record a video appeal to Vladimir Putin — in his video, he repeats Putin’s name more than once, saying that all his former written requests addressed to Putin had been forwarded to the ministry of defence, but he got no answers from them. (Video in the comments below.) There are literally thousands injured soldiers like him — only in 2023, over 140,000 more applications were filed in Russia with requests for wheelchairs and prosthetics. In Moscow, police has been raiding streets since Putin’s “inauguration”, grabbing young men and taking them to military recruitment offices. The men are put through the commission of medics, found “fit for military service” (despite many of them having chronic health conditions included on the list of diseases with which people shouldn’t be drafted), and sent to military units. Those who already had documents with the military where it’s recorded that they are ill, are still detained and not allowed to leave. The men are told they would have to serve in the army anyway, and they better sign that they agree to do it. At a the military office on Ugreshskaya Street, several dozen conscripts who are unfit or partially fit for service are being forcibly detained. Their family members came to the place and recorded video messages demanding the release of the men. Looks like while the Russian media promotes “overwhelming support” for Putin’s invasion, not many Russians are willing to allow their family members anywhere near the army. And those who survived the meat grinder of the Ukrainian front aren’t having much support — not even now, while Putin still needs great PR for the war in Ukraine. Imagine what’s going to happen when the war is over and those who lost their health there become an annoying reminder of the biggest blunder in the recent history of Russia. If you remember, Stalin loaded maimed WWII veterans in paddy wagons and shipped them to remote islands and locations that they couldn’t leave — so that the streets of the Soviet cities weren’t disturbed by the unsightly invalids, forced to beg to survive. That’s where these invalids died. They were sent there to die. And that was the war that the Soviets bragged they have “won”.

Why was Russia's counterattack weak in the face of Ukraine's offensive in Kursk? TAP ON THE PHOTO TO VIEW. Photo of the day: captured Russian conscripts are kneeling in front of a Ukrainian soldier. Russians in the border regions — both the troops and the civilians — aren’t resisting, because Russian citizens are trained to be passive. They don’t do anything without a command from the above, and once the Ukrainians shut down communications in an area, the Russians are staying idle, without their superiors yelling at them to motivate. By August 12, over 1,000 Russian soldiers have already surrendered to the Ukrainian troops in the Kursk region — the captives also include units of Russia’s FSB. The number of Russian captives starts posing a logistical problem for advancing Ukrainian troops: the captives need to be transported, fed, guarded. (Video in the comments below.) When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, unarmed Ukrainians were standing against tanks and soldiers with machine guns. Now, civilians in Russia don’t even attempt to resist. But it doesn’t mean there is no fighting in the Kursk region. The situation in Kursk hospitals and morgues is critical — too many bodies and wounded. "They are transporting the wounded in batches, the killed in batches, all the cars and KamAZ trucks are filled with corpses and "300s" without limbs. When a truck drives in, blood just flows out of it,” locals report. Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Syrsky posted a photo in which he is looking at the situation on the battlefield, accompanied by the words, “Continuing the operation." One thing that the Ukrainians are now saying, with a muted smirk, “We haven’t even started yet.” And that’s what Russians are really afraid of.

What are some things that Russians should start doing immediately? Panic is setting in Moscow and St. Petersburg: Russians are lining up to currency exchange booths, after the news broke about the latest US sanctions, which caused immediate suspension of currency trading on the Moscow Exchange. In short, the ruble is going bust. Some Russian banks set radical exchange rates of 50 rub. to buy and 200 rub. to sell, for USD $1. Others lifted the rates incrementally — that’s the banks that people are queuing to. Moscow bank branches have run out of cash. This morning, a correspondent from the Moscow Times visited almost two dozen branches of large banks (mainly Sberbank, but also Alfa and Avangard), but none of them had dollars. During the rampaging inflation of 1990s, Russia went through 10,000% inflation. One dollar was worth 6 rub. at the start, and near 6,000 rub. in 1997. As the result, the Moscow Exchange announced the suspension of trading in dollars and euros from June 13. The official ruble-dollar exchange rate will be now set by the Central Bank. In fact, yesterday the ruble has ceased to be a convertible currency. Putin wanted to revive the USSR, it seems that he’s getting there, in terms of currency exchange. In addition, the USA imposed sanctions against the divisions of Promsvyazbank, Vnesheconombank, Sberbank and VTB in Beijing, Hong Kong and India. These were the few branches that allowed exporters and importers to conduct financial transactions, to continue the flow of parts and goods to Russia. Now this back door is shut. On top of that, Russia has been banned from using all foreign technologies in the IT sector — the U.S. banned the supply of any software to Russia, even for individuals. On August 23, 1939, two criminal regimes — organizers of World War 2, Germany and the Soviet Union, signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and its secret protocol, defining the split of European territories between them. The pact gave the final impetus to the new world war, which began just 8 days later, with Germany’s attack on Poland. Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact: German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop (left), Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and USSR Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov (right) on August 23, 1939 in the Kremlin after signing the pact. Stalin made a toast after the ceremony: "I know how much the German people love their Fuhrer. Therefore, I want to drink to his health." On September 1, 1939 Germany’s attacked Poland. The Soviet Union attacked Poland on September 17, 1939. On September 22, Nazis and Soviets held a joint parade in Brest, celebrating their victory. For 50 years, the USSR leaders denied that there was a secret appendix to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. In 1946, at the Nuremberg Trials, the former State Secretary of the German Foreign Ministry, Ernst von Weizsäcker, spoke about the existence of a secret additional protocol between the USSR and Germany. This was confirmed by other defendants, and one of the lawyers even wanted to read the text of this protocol, but he was not allowed: the USSR representatives called it a fake and said such a document never existed. In 1948, the secret protocol, based on photocopies of the German original that had not survived, was published in the US State Department collection "Nazi-Soviet Relations. 1939-1941". It also included the correspondence between Nazi and Soviet diplomats, which contained references to secret agreements. But the Soviet Union continued to claim that this was a falsification, that no additional secret appendix to the 1939 agreements ("On Non-Aggression" and "On Friendship and Borders") between the USSR and Germany existed. Moreover: in response to the publication by the State Department, Moscow published its own work titled "Falsifiers of History". But it did not contain a single complete copy of a document, only a few fragments. Stalin didn’t want to be blamed in starting the World War with Hitler, and used the status of the USSR as one of the “victors of WW2” to suppress this extremely important information. Molotov, who signed the non-aggression pact and the secret protocol to it, denied its existence until his death in 1986. Minister of Foreign Affairs of the USSR Vyacheslav Molotov in Berlin, November 14, 1940. It was hard to prove that such a document existed: one party that signed it (Hitler's Germany) no longer existed, and the other (the Soviet Union) denied that it existed at all, and had no intention of publishing it. Only in 1989, the Soviet leaders admitted that such secret protocol existed, on request of representatives of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. A copy of the German document was published in the USSR. The actual copy of the secret protocol in Russian was first kept in Stalin's safe and then in the archive of the Central Committee of the Communist Party. In 1992, after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the archive of the Communist Party was declassified and the secret protocol was discovered. From that moment, the existence of a secret additional treaty to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact had become a reliably recognized fact not only in the West, not only in the Baltic countries, Moldova and Ukraine, but also in Russia itself. But now, Putin’s propaganda downplays the importance of the secret agreement between Hitler and Stalin how they would divide Europe, and overemphasizes that it was a non-aggression pact, which allowed the USSR 2 more years without the war. Completely disregarding the fact that without the secret agreement to split European lands, there possibly wouldn’t happen such a war.
